Accordingly, I visited the plantation and renewed my questioning among the older Black people there. At last, one of the oldest women told me she had heard of a spot called Bessop’s Castle and believed she could lead me to it. It was, however, neither a castle nor a tavern, but a lofty rock.

‘I promised her ample payment for her trouble, and after some hesitation she agreed to go with me. We reached the spot with little difficulty; then, having sent her away, I began my inspection. The “castle” was an irregular collection of cliffs and rocks, one of which was striking both for its height and for its detached, seemingly artificial form. I climbed to the top and found myself considerably puzzled about what to do next.

‘As I stood reflecting, I noticed a narrow ledge on the rock’s eastern face, perhaps a yard beneath the summit where I stood. It jutted out some eighteen inches and measured no more than a foot across. A recess in the cliff immediately above gave it a rough likeness to an ancestral chair with a hollow back. I had no doubt that I had found the “devil’s seat” mentioned in the manuscript, and now I seemed to possess the entire key to the riddle.

‘The “good glass,” I knew, must mean a telescope, for sailors seldom use the word “glass” in another sense. I understood at once that a telescope was required here, and that there was one fixed and unalterable position from which it must be used. Nor did I doubt that “forty-one degrees and thirteen minutes” and “northeast and by north” supplied instructions for directing the instrument. Much excited by what I had discovered, I hurried home, obtained a telescope, and came back to the rock.

‘I lowered myself onto the ledge and discovered that I could remain seated there in only one particular posture. This confirmed my earlier supposition. I then put the glass to use. Plainly, “forty-one degrees and thirteen minutes” could refer only to the elevation above the visible horizon, as the horizontal bearing was explicitly given by “northeast and by north.” With a pocket-compass I immediately determined that bearing. Then, raising the telescope as nearly as I could judge to an elevation of forty-one degrees, I shifted it carefully upward and downward until my eye was caught by a round gap, or opening, among the leaves of a great tree which stood taller than its neighbours in the distance.

My father had been the life within my life, and his memory remained so. I might be grateful to another, but never again could I love or hope as formerly; all was pain, and even my pleasures were borne rather than enjoyed. I resembled a lonely hollow among mountains, enclosed on every side by sheer black cliffs, into which no warmth could enter and from which no path led to sunnier meadows. Thus, although friendship’s spirit brought me brief comfort, it could not revive me. It arrived like a gentle visitation; it departed, and I scarcely noticed its loss. The animating spirit had died within me. Do not wonder, then, that I greeted heaven’s choicest gift—a friend—with no greater joy on its arrival, nor mourned more bitterly when it went.

My friend’s name was Woodville. I shall tell his history briefly, that you may judge the coldness of a heart unmoved by his eloquence and tender sympathy, and understand how, being himself deeply unhappy, he and I were suited to console one another, had Misery’s Medusa-head not turned me into stone. Woodville’s sorrows did not strike the heart’s centre as mine did; his grief was natural, destined to cleanse rather than destroy the heart. Once its shadow lifted from him, he might emerge with greater happiness and brightness than before.

Woodville was a poor clergyman’s son and had been educated in the classics. He belonged to that tiny number whom fortune blesses from birth, lavishing gifts of mind and person upon them without limit, and sheltering them so specially that no blemish, however slight, nor disappointment, however passing, is permitted to approach. She seemed to have fashioned his mind from an excellence no impurity could stain, and given him an understanding which no falsehood could lead astray. His genius surpassed all measure; when it appeared, like a brilliant star rising in the east, every eye turned towards it in admiration. He was a Poet. That title has been so frequently debased that it cannot express the fullness of what he was. He resembled some ancient poet whom the muses had garlanded in his cradle, and upon whose lips the bees had fed. Moving among other men, he appeared surrounded by a celestial halo that set him apart and raised him above them. His extraordinary beauty, the flashing ardour of his eyes, and the rich music of words that held his hearers in silent, ecstatic wonder, made him tower above all others, until beside him they seemed created only to attend upon his higher excellence.

Were our lofty dreams to vanish in this manner? We had been placed ‘a little lower than the angels’; yet behold, we proved no more enduring than mayflies. We had styled ourselves the ‘paragon of animals,’ and now were revealed as a ‘quint-essence of dust.’ We lamented that the pyramids survived their builder’s embalmed remains. Alas! even the shepherd’s straw hut we passed beside the road possessed, in its humble construction, the prospect of outlasting the entire human race. How could this sorrowful reversal be reconciled with our former aspirations, our seeming strength?

Suddenly a voice within me appeared to speak, distinctly and clearly: So it was ordained from eternity; the horses drawing Time onward have borne this hour and this fulfilment chained to them since the void delivered its burden. Would you reverse the immutable laws of Necessity?

Mother of the world! Attendant upon the Almighty! everlasting, unalterable Necessity, whose tireless fingers continually weave the unbreakable chain of events! I shall not complain of your deeds. If my mortal understanding cannot assent that whatever exists is right, still, since whatever exists must exist, I shall sit smiling among the ruins. Indeed, we were born not for enjoyment, but for submission and hope.

Would the reader grow weary if I described in detail our protracted journey from Paris to Geneva? Were I to set down daily, as in a journal, the miseries that crowded upon us, could my hand record, or language provide expressions for, our manifold sufferings, the pressing succession of one dreadful occurrence after another? Be patient, reader, whoever you may be, wherever your dwelling lies, whether you belong to a spiritual race or, descended from some surviving pair, possess a human nature and inhabit the earth. Here you will read the actions of a vanished people and wonder whether those who endured these recorded things were made of delicate flesh and fragile substance like yourself. Indeed they were. Weep, then; surely, solitary creature, your disposition will be gentle. Let tears of compassion fall, but listen meanwhile to the story and learn what your predecessors did and suffered.

Yet the closing events of our passage through France held such peculiar horror and sombre wretchedness that I dare not linger over their telling. Were I to examine every incident, each tiny division of a second would yield a tale of anguish whose smallest word would freeze the blood in your youthful veins. It is fitting that I raise this memorial to the departed race for your instruction; it is not fitting that I lead you through hospital wards or the hidden chambers of the house of death.
